Run Facebook and Instagram in the US, aimed at homeowners 35+, on weekdays as the advertiser prefers. That helps hit the contact-rate and credit-check targets. Track which angle performs best: cash from your home, a lower rate, or the veterans angle.

notes.mediaTakeaways:
This is a Facebook and Instagram game in the US, and Quicken and Rocket's own ads take up most of the space. Several affiliates already send traffic to this exact Quicken page. Other lead-gen players, like BestMoney and QuoteAssist, run their own quizzes and comparison pages.

Native is a second real channel for this vertical. Quicken itself buys Outbrain traffic to its own comparison pages, where it sits on top and Rocket, AmeriSave and loanDepot appear as sponsored results. Publishers run HELOC advertorials on Taboola, Mgid and Outbrain (Comparisons.org, Bankerology), and MSN carries rate-quiz and top-10 list pages (Lendgo, Mortgage-Insiders). There is also some search-arbitrage traffic on refinance keywords. Hometap, Figure and Finance of America only show their pages to US visitors.

There are few new big native buyers; the large refi and HELOC native spenders are listed above. notes.mediaTakeaways:
Taboola carries most of this traffic, and Outbrain is a solid second. Outbrain is especially strong for skin, hair, toenail and men's offers. MGID shows up mostly as an extra source, and NewsBreak is used in the US for the most aggressive health claims.

Nearly every offer uses the same path: the ad leads to an article or review page, and that page sends people to the product. A few memory offers use a video sales letter instead of a written article, a few skin offers add a short quiz, and only a couple (like Temu) send people straight to the store.

Some offers have been running for a very long time: a TV streaming stick for well over a year, and a toenail product, a cleaning cloth, a neuropathy device and a pillow for four to six months each. Those are the proven ones.

notes.mediaTakeaways:
This is all Facebook and Instagram, US, aimed at men over 40. Most of the volume comes from affiliates using pages that look like regular people or small health pages. They send clicks straight to the QUAD site or right into the sign-up quiz.

The longer-lasting setup is different: an ad leads to a "men's health" article comparing QUAD with Hims, Roman and other brands, and the article sends readers on to buy. Those are the ads that have stayed live for over a month.

The big players scale by running the same ad 2–3 times and pushing out new versions almost daily.
notes.creativeActions: Start with what's clearly working: short videos of a woman holding the bottle with an age callout, and make several versions of each one. Take a script that already works and put it over different footage instead of writing new scripts every time. A simple "pill takes an hour, QUAD takes 10 minutes" comparison is worth testing, as is leading with the price per use. For traffic going to an article, reuse the "men are quitting Viagra" style images. Keep the claims clean so ads and pages don't get shut down.
notes.creativeTakeaways:
QUAD is a new product, and almost everything running for it is short vertical video, most of it launched in the last few weeks. The most common ad is an AI-made "real woman" holding the bottle and calling out an age ("Born before 1962?"). Next to that are simple talking heads (a wife, a pharmacist, an older guy) and animated bottle videos.

The message barely changes from ad to ad: it works in 10–15 minutes, lasts up to 36 hours, and it's a liquid under the tongue, so no pill and no waiting after food. Many ads also take a shot at Viagra and Cialis and mention the price.

The ads that have lasted longest aren't videos. They're simple news-style images ("This is why men are quitting Viagra") that lead to a review article.
